content.text: The excerpt combines John Evelyn’s diary (1694–1705) with medical treatises on membranous enteritis, dysentery, typhlitis, intestinal ulcers, hemorrhage, and obstruction. Evelyn records politics, war, religious controversies, epidemics, weather, deaths, libraries, art, and the founding of Greenwich Hospital. He moved from Sayes Court to Wotton, visited London, Deptford, Lambeth, Greenwich, Eton, Oxford, Kensington, and numerous country estates. The Czar of Muscovy stayed at Sayes Court, using it as his court and palace. The medical sections describe intestinal inflammation, mucus-rich exudates, dysenteric symptoms, causes, pathology, complications, prognosis, sanitation, diet, irrigation, opium, ipecacuanha, and surgery. They emphasize contaminated water and excreta, climate, overcrowding, and the dangers of obstruction, perforation, hemorrhage, and delayed laparotomy.
